s06.slug: MONDAY · 2:35 PM · THE SAAB, OCEAN ROAD → THE 101 SOUTH
body: The rain is coming in off the Channel in gray sheets, one behind another, walking up over the bluff and flattening the ice plant on their way inland, and at the Marine Lab turnout the chain across the service drive is streaming. The Saab is nosed up to it with the top up. Up, the top is mostly tape: silver along one seam, black along the next, and over the passenger side a strip of blue painter’s tape where somebody ran out of both.

He gets in with the umbrella fighting him to the last rib, and the blazer folded over his arm, dry except for one cuff. Skye is behind the wheel in a man’s raincoat with the sleeves turned back four times, over something pink and quilted that he looks at once — “Don’t,” she says — and her hair is wound up on her head with a Sharpie stuck through the knot. A paperback *Little Women* is on his seat with a gas receipt in it about a third of the way through. She moves it to the dash as he sits.
“Beth’s still alive,” she says. “I’m reading slow.”
She looks up at the canvas over their heads. It shudders every time the wind gets under a seam. “The rule is top down,” she says. “The rule has met the rain.”

At the light by the on-ramp the roof finds his left knee. One cold drop through the seam over his head, then another in the same place, then another, steady as a kitchen faucet with a bad washer, into the denim. The defroster is blowing at the windshield as hard as it can and losing; she wipes a porthole in the fog with the raincoat’s cuff and drives through that.

South of town the 101 goes down through Gaviota Pass between walls of black rock with water coming off them in ropes, and comes out along the Channel, and the afternoon goes gray in layers: the road, the water beside the road, the place where the islands ought to be. Trucks throw up spray that hangs behind them like smoke. She drives fast anyway, in the left lane, both hands on the wheel.

“It’s a camera test,” she says, when he asks. “Not an audition. I already got through the audition. Now they need to know if the camera likes me in a dress from 1962 when I’m sad.” She passes a horse trailer with a horse’s rear end in it, resigned to the weather. “The camera has always liked me sad. It’s a whole problem.”
“Which scene?”
“The last one. The rain.”
“She forgives him.”

“In forty buttons.” She takes a hand off the wheel and draws a line from her throat down to her lap. “Here’s your character. You’re my cousin from Ohio. You’ve come out to see the industry. You’re very shy and you wash dishes.”
“I do wash dishes.”
“That’s what makes it work.” She makes a small, exact shape in the air with her fingers. “*Specificity.*”

Past Refugio the white iPhone lights up in the cup holder and says MOM. She lets it ring once and most of a second time. Her thumb goes to the speaker and stops there, and she picks the phone up instead and wedges it between her ear and her shoulder and puts both hands back on the wheel.
“Hi, Mom.”
He has never heard her sound like this: brighter, quicker, half a step up, a girl answering the phone in somebody’s kitchen with her homework done.

“Driving. No, I’m being careful. I’m in the slow lane.” She is in the fast lane. “Wednesday’s fine. What time? I’ll be there. I’ll eat first.” She listens. A green sign goes over them, unreadable in the rain. “The reunion picture? Everybody? Sure. Sure, Mom, that’s fine.” She listens longer. The wipers go.

None of the bright goes out of it. “She changed it *back*?” Jack looks out at the Channel. “No. No, it’s fine. *New Moon* is fine.” She laughs, a pleasant laugh that would go over well on any phone. “I know she does. Tell her thanks.” A truck passes on the right and throws a sheet of water over the glass, and she drives blind through it without a flicker. “Love you, Mom.”

She drops the phone back in the cup holder with the screen to the seat, and drives a mile. On the curve past El Capitan *Little Women* slides across the dash toward him, and she reaches out and puts it back where it was, and keeps her hand on it till the road straightens.

A Ralphs truck comes up on the right, throwing spray, and she lifts her chin at it. “Gil,” she says, in her own voice. “Married to a woman who picks out his shirts. He hasn’t chosen a shirt since 1979, and if you asked him what color he likes, he’d have to call home.”

At Carpinteria the flags over a car lot hang at half-staff for Pearl Harbor, too wet to stir. At the Rincon the road runs along a shelf of boulders with the ocean right up against it, and today the ocean is coming over. The surf throws itself up the riprap gray and white and slides back off across the shoulder in sheets, and she moves them over a lane. Ventura goes by low and wet. Past it, where the road leaves the water and starts across the flat green fields toward the hills, she finds a station that comes in, and turns it up.

It’s a woman singing high and quick over a guitar, about being a long way off somewhere and wanting not to be, and Skye knows every word. Jack doesn’t know it at all. When it comes around to *coming home* she sings it at the windshield, under the woman, low, with her eyes on the road, and her face is younger than it was on the phone, and not in the same way.

On the Conejo Grade the wind comes across the hills broadside and leans on the car, and the canvas over his head snaps and fills, and the blue tape over the seam lifts at one corner. The drip on his knee is a thin, steady stream now. She sees it. She keeps climbing.

response: “The camera tolerates cousins,” she says. “Don’t look straight at it. It thinks that’s an invitation.”

choices.text: “You sounded about twelve on the phone.”
response: She keeps her eyes on the road. “Eleven,” she says. “That’s when I started.” A wiper’s length. “Don’t do that, Ohio. You’ll ruin my makeup, and I’m not wearing any.”

choices.text: Say nothing. Find the leak and hold the tape.
response: He reaches up and finds the loose corner of the blue tape and presses it back over the seam, his hand flat on her roof, and holds it there. She looks at his arm up over his head, holding her car together, and laughs through her nose, and drives the rest of the Grade like that.

body: Burbank in the rain at twenty to six is every gutter on the block running at once. The block is warehouses: a prop house with a fiberglass horse in its fenced yard under a blue tarp, a lumber yard with its gate chained, and in the middle a long beige building with no windows and a 9 painted on its side three stories tall.
A guard sits at the gate in a plywood shed with a space heater going at his shins. He slides his window back and looks at her and nowhere else. “Evening, Miss Callender. Some night.”
“My cousin from Ohio,” Skye says.

Only then does the guard look past her, at Jack in the passenger seat with one wet knee. He runs his pen down a list on his clipboard to a line — CALLENDER, S. + 1 — and holds out a paper visitor pass with a clip on it. She takes it, pulls the Sharpie out of her hair, writes on the pass in capitals against the steering wheel, pushes the Sharpie back into the knot, and hands it to Jack. MY COUSIN FROM OHIO.
“Where people can see it,” she says.
Over the stage door there’s a red bulb in a wire cage, dark. “When that’s on, you don’t open the door. You don’t sneeze. You don’t be from anywhere.”

Inside, the storm is louder. It’s on the roof, three stories up, a hard steady roar over the dark of the grid, and under the grid, under a hundred lamps hung off pipes, somebody has built 1962. A canvas revival tent stands in the middle of the stage with one side rolled up: a sawdust aisle between rows of folding chairs, a piano with the ivory gone off two keys, a plywood pulpit, and over it a banner in house paint, JESUS SAVES — ALL WELCOME. Through the tent’s far flap a parking lot is painted on the floor with three cars from the year on it — a Ford, a Studebaker with its chrome taped over so it won’t flare, a pickup with a dog crate in the bed — and over the cars, on a crane arm, a rain tower: a row of pipes with sprinkler heads in it, dripping from the last test into a plastic kiddie pool somebody has set under the worst of it. It is going to rain in here tonight, under a roof that’s being rained on. Jack seems to be the only one who thinks that’s funny.

Wardrobe takes her. When she comes back she’s in a cape at a mirror beside the tent with a woman setting her hair into 1962, pins in the woman’s mouth, and from then on the stage wants things from her, one after another, and Jack stands behind the mirror and watches them come.

The hair woman takes the pins out of her mouth and holds out a flip phone with stickers on it. “My niece’s. She’s twelve. She made me bring it. Would you —” “Say it like Cassidy?” Skye takes the phone and thumbs through to the greeting, and out of her comes somebody else entirely, sweet and a half-step high, a girl from a lake who hopes you’re having a nice day. *Hi! You’ve reached Brianna! She can’t come to the phone, but she’s so glad you called.* It’s perfect. The hair woman puts a hand over her heart.

A producer’s assistant, with a magazine — her face on the cover from some summer, a bikini top and a great deal of lip gloss — and a silver pen. *To Kayla’s mom.* An agent’s assistant, holding out a phone: a car service will be at the gate at one to take her home. “I drove.” “They’re sending it anyway.” “Then it can follow me.” A grip with a sandbag on his shoulder whose nephew has written a script, a really good one, about a dog that solves crimes. She writes the nephew’s email on the back of her hand.

And all through it people raise their phones. A BlackBerry, a Motorola, somebody’s iPhone held sideways. Every time one comes up her face goes to the same place for it — chin down, eyes up, the smile — and holds there for the click, and comes back.

Jack finds the coffee, a long table against the wall with a man in an apron guarding the shrimp, and the man in the apron looks at his blazer and asks if he’s network. “Cousin,” Jack says. The man reads his lapel. “Ohio,” he says, with real sympathy, and lets him have a shrimp. Jack brings her a coffee, black, and puts it in her hand under the cape. When a PA gives her two stapled pages to look at while her hair sets, she can’t hold them and the coffee both, so he holds the pages up at her eye level and turns to the second one when she nods. “My sides,” she says. “You’re holding my sides.” Once a PA going by hands him a coil of cable and points, and he carries it where the PA pointed and comes back, and in the mirror she watches him go and come back with her coffee stopped halfway to her mouth. When the last phone goes down she finds him in the mirror, behind her with page two, and her face is the one from the car.

The director comes through in a scarf, indoors, and frames the tent with his fingers, and frames her, and once, passing, frames Jack. The boy who plays the thief is twenty-two, with a face Jack is fairly sure he has seen on the side of a bus. He shakes Jack’s hand and calls him cuz. He calls him cuz again on his way past with a plate of shrimp, and seems prepared to keep it up all night.

At ten past seven the first AD, a small woman with a radio on each hip, comes into video village with a problem. The boy’s stand-in is on the 405, and the 405 is a parking lot, and the cinematographer needs a body about six feet tall on the thief’s mark under the rain, now, so he can light Miss Callender’s face against it before they lose the hour. She says this into one of her radios. She is looking at Jack while she says it. So is the cinematographer. So, from the hair chair with pins in her head, is Skye.

choices.key: In Burbank, in the first storm of the winter, you stood under a rain tower in your blazer so they could light her face.
response: They put him on a piece of tape by the Studebaker and turn the rain on. It comes out of the pipes colder than the real thing on the roof, and in about four seconds he is wet to the skin in the Goodwill blazer, water running off his nose, while forty people with ladders and light meters light the girl across from him. She’s on her mark under an umbrella a PA holds over her, in the raincoat over the dress, and for nine minutes by the clock on the slate she doesn’t take her eyes off him. When they cut the water she’s the first one there with a towel.

choices.key: In Burbank they needed a body in the rain. You told them you’re union.
response: The crew laughs, the first AD loudest, and the grip with the nephew puts down his sandbag and goes and stands on the mark himself and gets rained on for nine minutes with his arms folded. Between setups Skye finds Jack in the glow of the monitors and mouths it at him across the stage: *union*.

choices.key: In Burbank they needed a body in the rain. You stayed behind the monitor — just the cousin.
response: He stays behind the monitor. A grip stands in, arms folded, and gets rained on. Every time the bell rings for a new setup she looks for Jack there first, and every time he’s there.

body: The honeywagon is a long white trailer parked against the side of the stage, chopped into rooms the width of a closet, and hers has SKYE on the door on a strip of tape. Inside there’s a mirror ringed in bulbs, a vinyl bench, a counter of pins and powder, and a window the size of a paperback with the rain sheeting down it. The rain on the trailer roof is closer than the rain on the stage, and louder, like sitting inside a drum.

She’s in the dress. White cotton, sleeves to the wrist, a collar that stands up under her jaw, and down the front of it, from the hem to the throat, forty buttons covered in the same white cotton, every one of them done.
“Forty,” she says. “Hem to chin. They didn’t want anybody getting to her before the end of the second act.” She shuts the door with her heel.
She backs him onto the squeaking bench and comes down after him with a knee on either side of him on the vinyl and the skirt going everywhere, yards of it, over his legs and the bench and the floor.

body.text: He’s still wet. The blazer is soaked through and his shirt is stuck to him under it, and she takes a lapel in each fist and wrings them out, hard, onto the floor of the trailer. “Nine minutes,” she says. “I’ve been waiting nine minutes to do that.”
body.else: He’s dry. She checks, both hands inside the blazer at his ribs, and seems to think it’s a waste.

body: Her lipstick is somebody’s idea of 1962, a dark rose, and it’s on him almost at once, and she lets it be. When his hand goes to her collar she catches it. “No buttons,” she says against his mouth. “Wardrobe counted them. They’ll *know*.”

So his hands go everywhere the buttons aren’t. The small of her back, warm through the cotton. Her wrists, where the sleeves end and her pulse is going under his thumbs. Her jaw, and the soft place under it where the collar stops and his mouth can get to. The backs of her knees under the hem, bare, where she makes a sound into his neck that isn’t in anybody’s script.

She keeps score. Every time his hand strays toward the front of the dress she calls the button by its number — “Nine. Careful. *Twenty-two*” — and the numbers get worse on purpose, until by her count the dress has sixty-one buttons and he has been near every one of them. She’s laughing against his mouth; she stops laughing. She kisses him slower, and harder, with both hands in his hair and her weight coming down on him through all that cotton, and he holds her by the backs of the knees and forgets what number they were on. He wants her badly enough to say so and hasn’t got the breath to.

Somebody knocks on the trailer door, three times, polite. Through the little window the somebody is a yellow rain slicker under an umbrella, waiting on the metal step. “Skye? They’re ready for you in the rain.”

“Coming,” she says, in an entirely reasonable voice, with one hand still in his hair. Then she’s up and at the mirror, fixing a collar that was never crooked, running a finger down the front of the dress and counting under her breath, and getting forty. She does her mouth in one stroke. She looks at his in the mirror. “Makeup’s going to have questions.”
She has her hand on the latch.

choices.text: Catch her wrist at the door.
response: He catches her wrist, and she turns around into it, and it’s once more, hard, against the trailer door, with the PA standing on the other side of it on the metal step. “*Cousin*,” she says into his mouth, and goes.

choices.text: “I’d like to stay in here all night.”
response: She stops with her hand on the latch and looks back at him on the bench, under the bulbs, with her lipstick on him. “People in this trailer say *how long have we got*,” she says, and goes out into the rain to forgive somebody.

choices.text: Let her go. Sit there till your heart slows.
response: She goes. He sits on the vinyl in the ring of bulbs with the rain on the roof. In the mirror there’s a man in a Goodwill blazer with a girl’s 1962 lipstick on his mouth, and Jack looks at him until his heart slows.

s07b.slug: MONDAY · 10:30 PM · STAGE 9, THE TENT IN THE RAIN
body: Take four. The rain comes out of the pipes in a white curtain under the lamps, loud on the painted asphalt, and through it the preacher’s daughter comes out of the tent and finds the boy who stole from the plate, standing by the Studebaker with the money in his fist. She says his name. He turns around. She forgives him, and she cries.

Jack has never watched her act before. She’s good. Nothing extra and everything where it goes, like his father under a hood. The tears come when she wants them, on the word she wants them on, and run down the same cheek the same way, take after take. Take five, the same. The made rain makes its own weather: a cold mist drifts off it as far as video village and settles on the monitors, and between takes a PA goes down the row wiping the screens with a chamois, so that every time Jack watches her cry he watches it through somebody’s wiping. After each one the director comes out of his chair and goes to her in the rain with his palms pressed together, and when the water shuts off Jack can hear what he says, because it’s the same every time. *More grace. Give me more grace.* Jack has been asking for the same thing since the second grade. He never thought to try it in a scarf.

body.text: Jack watches from video village in a borrowed crew jacket three sizes wrong, his blazer hung on a light stand behind him, dripping onto the cables.

body: Before take five the boy who plays the thief comes to video village with water running out of his hair and leans in at Jack’s elbow. “Cuz. Is she always this good?” “Since she was eleven,” Jack says, which is true as far as he knows it, and the boy nods, satisfied, at the family history. While they reset the rain they bring her to the monitors in a towel. She stands at Jack’s shoulder behind the director’s chair with her hair dripping on the white cotton and watches herself cry on the playback, and when it’s done she says, low, for him only: “What. You’re making a face.”

choices.text: “Nobody forgives anybody in the rain. You forgive somebody the next morning, when it’s dry and nobody’s watching and it costs something.”
response: She stops toweling. She looks at him out of the towel while the rain comes back on behind her. The bell goes for take six, and she walks out into it.

choices.text: “She’s crying because she’s sad. She should be tired. Forgiving somebody is mostly being tired of it.”
response: She hears it out with the towel at her ear. She nods once, slowly, as she did at her pages in the hair chair, and drops the towel over his arm, and the bell goes for take six.
“Liar,” she says, and hands him the towel. The bell goes for take six.

body: Take six: the bell, the red light outside, the rain coming down out of the pipes. On the monitor she comes out of the tent and finds the boy by the Studebaker the same as five times before, and she doesn’t cry.

She’s tired. She looks at the boy across the rain like she has been up all night with what he did and has come out the far side of it, and she reaches up and does the top button of his collar against the wet, one button, with her fingers stiff from the cold. She says the line flat and kind. “It’s all right, Lonnie. Go on home and get dry.” Like it’s the next morning. Like it costs something to say, and she’s paying it.

body.text: Jack hears his own sentence come back to him with her face on it.
body.else: It’s the face he made at the monitor. She’s playing that.

body: The stage goes quiet the way St. Brendan’s goes at the consecration, the crew holding still at once, ladders and all, and there’s only the rain on the roof until the director says “Cut,” so softly it barely counts.
He’s out of his chair. “What was *that*?”
Skye has her face in a towel. “My cousin,” she says, into it.
The director turns around in his scarf and finds Jack behind the monitors. “You act?”
“I wash dishes.”
Behind him the boy who plays the thief, dripping, points at Jack and says, “Cuz,” like it settles something.
At two minutes past eleven, in the dark at the back of video village, the phone goes against his leg.

body.text: Book Nine is 566 lines and I know all of them. Pray for me at 8. —L.

body: He reads it with the screen turned in against his chest, where the light can’t go anywhere, and doesn’t answer it yet.

They wrap at twenty to one. The real rain has stopped, and somebody has shut off the other one. Under the rain tower, dead now and dripping into its kiddie pool, she stands in the man’s raincoat with a garment bag over her shoulder and the Sharpie back in her hair.
“Was that my world?”
“That was a Monday.”

At the gate the guard slides his window back. “Night, Miss Callender. Night, cousin.” Jack wishes him a good night in the voice of a shy man who washes dishes, and she laughs about it till the freeway.

The 101 north is empty and black and shining. Ventura goes by wet, every light in it doubled on the road. She drives with both hands and doesn’t sing. He doesn’t sleep, though twice she tells him he’s allowed.

He types it low against the door while she keeps her eyes on the road. At twenty to four she stops short of the chain at the Marine Lab turnout and lets him out into the dripping ice plant with the engine running and the pass still clipped to his lapel.
